Enhancing sensitivity through optimization of the measurement and sample preparation conditions the achievable dipolar evolution time was extended to 150 µs. Thus, distances close to 20 nm should become experimentally accessible, highlighting the potential of advanced PDS methodologies for probing previously inaccessible long-range structural information in complex systems.
items.authors: Yannik Limbach, Katrin Ackermann, Aisika Chakraborty, David G. Norman, Bela E. Bode

items.title: Closing the Loop Between Synthetic and Living Cells
items.abstract: Synthetic cells are moving beyond compartmentalised microreactors to become integrated components of biological networks that physically and chemically merge with their hosts. Existing reviews classify this field by mode of emission, by chemistry, or by architecture, and so describe the construct rather than its effect. This review takes the receiver's side, treating the functional adaptation of the living host as the readout of bio-hybrid function: how living cells probe their synthetic partners mechanically and adapt to them metabolically. We consider the bio-hybrid interface by how far the feedback loop (sensing-actuation) is closed and set out the evidence that would place a study in each of four tiers: open-loop, half-loop, partial feedback, and closed-loop. Read against these criteria, sixteen of the eighteen studies surveyed here are half-loop, two reach partial feedback, and none is closed-loop. Both partial-feedback systems work the same way, by metabolic interception, which the existing taxonomies have no category for. The one construct that comes closest to closed-loop operation contains no living cell at all. We then trace how single-cell coupling is scaling into hybrid prototissues that act as discovery platforms for pathological microenvironments, and we outline the translational barriers these constructs must survive to reach the clinic.
items.authors: Ion Ioannou

items.title: Sorting Commodity Plastics by MOF-based Molecular Sieving
items.abstract: Efficient sorting of waste plastics according to their chemical structure is desirable for plastics recycling. Here, we present a novel methodology based on a molecular sieving mechanism to realize molecular-level sorting of polymer chains. Using nanopores in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) as the sieve, polymer chains are differentiated by their thickness and branching structure through selective infiltration into the nanopores in the molten state. The infiltration process is evaluated in situ and semi-quantitatively via continuous monitoring of relative diffraction intensity from the MOF using variable-temperature X-ray diffraction. Three MOFs with varying effective pore window diameters are identified as promising candidates that enable sequential sorting of four highly important commodity plastics: low-density polyethylene, polystyrene, polypropylene, and high-density polyethylene. This work would open up a new paradigm in the field by providing a versatile method capable of sorting the waste plastics mixture with molecular-level precision.
items.authors: Haruaki Suzuki, Ryo Shimura, Nobuhiko Hosono, Takashi Uemura

items.title: Critical assessment of published Kalina cycle studies: cycle configuration, state-point reporting and optimisation bounds
items.abstract: The Kalina cycle is widely proposed for converting geothermal, solar and waste heat, including in systems that also supply cooling, fresh water or hydrogen. It differs from an ammonia–water Rankine cycle in two respects established in its original formulation: a separator that produces a working solution richer in ammonia than the basic solution, and internal recuperation of turbineexhaust heat. Three operational criteria were derived from these features: non-zero mass flow in both separator outlets, a working-to-basic ammonia mass-fraction difference of at least 0.05, and non-zero recuperator duty. These criteria, a ten-item reporting checklist and a comparison of reported optima with the published search bounds were applied to 88 full-text journal articles, 84 of which designate a cycle as a Kalina cycle. In 17 of the 84 studies (20%; 95% CI 13–30%), at least one designated Kalina layout contained no recuperator or no separator. At the operating point of the principal results, all three criteria were demonstrably satisfied in 19 studies (23%), at least one was violated in 20 (24%), and 45 (54%) reported insufficient data for a decision. A complete state-point table was reported in 20 of the 88 studies. Of 40 optimisations performed with a named algorithm, 22 reported both bounds and optimal values; in 18 of these, at least one optimum coincided with or exceeded a bound, including all 14 single-objective cases. Agreement between an initial and a blinded repeat scoring was substantial (κ = 0.69–0.77). A verification procedure and a minimum reporting set are proposed.
items.authors: Mohammad Masrur Hossain, Mohammad Mehran Hossain

items.title: An Ultrathin Embedded SnO2 Interface for Water Dissociation in Bipolar Membranes and pseudo-PEM Electrolyzers
items.abstract: Water dissociation (WD) at bipolar membrane (BPM) junctions is a key reaction in a number of electrochemical energy conversion and separation technologies. While metal oxide catalysts like SnO 2 accelerate WD, conventional particle-based deposition methods typically yield thick and morphologically heterogeneous junction layers. We report a simple aqueous precursor-treatment route that reconstructs the near-surface region of Nafion into an ultrathin SnO 2 -bearing interface. In contrast to conventional spin-coated SnO 2 , which forms a discrete particulate overlayer, the embedded interface is smooth, spatially confined, and closely integrated with the membrane. Despite this major structural difference, BPMs fabricated from SnO 2 -eb-Nafion exhibit WD performance comparable to benchmark spin-coated SnO 2 junctions. When normalized by SnO 2 loading, the embedded junction delivers a ~21-fold higher current density in an electrolyzer test cell at a total cell voltage of 2 V, highlighting improved catalyst utilization. Structural and electrochemical controls show that the high activity arises from interfacially localized SnO 2 rather than bulk SnO 2 incorporation or altered proton conductivity. The embedded route improves precursor efficiency, increases membrane junction adhesion force by 7×, and maintains stable operation under continuous elec-trolyzer testing. A preliminary pseudo-PEM water-electrolysis demonstration further shows that the embedded SnO 2 interface remains beneficial in an AEI–PEM heterojunction architecture coupled to a PGM-free Co 3 O 4 anode. These results establish precursor-based interfacial self-reconstruction as a practical route to thin, active, and mechanically integrated catalyst–membrane junctions. Keywords: Bipolar membranes; Water dissociation; Tin oxide (SnO 2 ); Ionomer interfaces; Water electrolysis
items.authors: Yifan Wu, Benjamin N. Indeglia, Vivek S. Devalla, Wenbo Zhang, Helen K. Chen, Peiyao Wu

items.title: Designing Ideal Denoisers for Chromatographic and Spectroscopic Signals
items.abstract: Modern instrumental analyses have different types of noise superimposed on the true signal, from low frequencies (baselines and colored noise) to very high-frequency components like sharp spikes. Convolution based denoisers or frequency domain filters inadequately handle colored noise and induce baseline oscillations while broadening narrow peaks. Herein, two new dataadaptive denoising methods are developed for chromatographic and spectroscopic data. The goal is to suppress noise without appreciably distorting peak shape or quantitative information (area, location, and variance). The proposed methods are posed as optimization problems inspired by the Bohlmann-Whittaker smoother. The objective function consists of a data fidelity term and adaptive second difference and bi-scale log-cosh penalties. The latter term suppresses pink or colored noise effectively, while adaptive functions protect narrow and weak peaks. The second method is designed for intensity-dependent additive and proportional noise and combines an inverse hyperbolic sine variance-stabilizing transformation with adaptive second-difference regularization. Non-uniform sampling rates are tolerated by this second smoother. In simulated chromatograms containing white and pink noise, the proposed adaptive method reduced the reconstruction error by approximately 40-50% relative to Gaussian weighted moving average and penalized least squares smoothing. The resolution of closely spaced peaks was maintained, and a weak peak with a weak peak with a signal-to-noise ratio near 5 was recovered. The proposed denoisers were evaluated on real data from GC-IMS, LC-MS/MS, Raman spectra relevant to planetary studies, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy of graphitic surface, and overloaded LC-MS instruments as test cases with and without baseline correction. Most denoiser parameters are derived from noise estimated from a single chromatogram or spectrum; no training or learning algorithms are required. The denoisers are fast and can be extended to 2D data.
items.authors: M. Farooq Wahab

items.title: Interpretable QSPR Modeling of Surfactant Characteristic Curvature
items.abstract: Characteristic curvature (Cc) quantifies the intrinsic interfacial curvature tendency of surfactants under defined reference conditions and is a key input to the hydrophilic–lipophilic deviation (HLD) framework for predicting microemulsion phase behavior; however, experimental determination remains laborious, and interpretable molecular structure–Cc relationships across diverse surfactant chemistries are comparatively underdeveloped. Here, we developed a quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) framework using a curated literature-derived dataset of 63 anionic and nonionic surfactants, with molecular structures verified against the original sources and experimental values curated to improve consistency of the Cc endpoint, and benchmarked multiple tree-based regression algorithms using two-dimensional RDKit descriptors, fold-contained preprocessing, Yeo–Johnson target transformation, SHAP-based feature selection, and nested cross-validation. XGBoost achieved the strongest performance on 13-surfactants test set, with R 2 = 0.85, RMSE = 0.53, and MAE = 0.44 Cc units, with all metrics calculated on the inverse-transformed scale; the observed error was of the same order of magnitude as reported experimental uncertainty, supporting preliminary prediction within the represented chemical domain rather than replacing experimental Cc determination. SHAP and partial-dependence analyses identified electrotopological, topological, hydrophobicity-related, and other physicochemical descriptors associated with the model response, revealing nonlinear and threshold-like patterns that support chemically interpretable structure–property hypotheses without establishing causal mechanisms or experimentally validated design rules; the framework therefore offers a reproducible basis for prioritizing structurally related surfactants for subsequent experimental evaluation and provides a methodological reference for future Cc modeling with broader chemical coverage and prospective validation.
items.authors: Affan Dulyadech, Uthaiporn Suriyapraphadilok, Ampira Charoensaeng, Natthapong Sueviriyapan

items.title: Polyethyleneimine (PEI) molecular weight alters the photophysical and FRET properties of water dispersible NaYF4:Yb,Er upconversion nanoparticles
items.abstract: Upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) are optically active materials with near-infrared excitation and tuneable anti-Stokes emission, typically resulting in visible emission. A route to routine and reliable synthesis of water-dispersible UCNPs for biomedical imaging applications is the polyethyleneimine (PEI)- assisted solvothermal autoclave synthesis; however, the properties of the resulting UCNPs remain understudied. Herein, we report how PEI molecular weight alters properties of core-only, red-emitting, water-dispersible PEI-UCNPs. In terms of brightness, 1.2 kDa PEI-UCNPs exhibited 5 times more intense upconversion luminescence (UCL) than 25 kDa PEI-UCNPs and a 29% longer UCL lifetime (LT) for the red emission band (~640-690 nm, 4 F 9/2 → 4 I 15/2 Er 3+ transition) in DI H 2 O. Dispersal in D 2 O increased emission across wavebands, with green emission ( 2 H 11/2 , 4 S 3/2 → 4 I 15/2 Er 3+ transition) increasing by 248 - 365% whereas red emission only increased between 38-64%. From our results, we infer that PEI may quench the UCL via high-energy NH vibrations. We also examined Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) between PEI-UCNPs and an electrostatically adsorbed fluorescent model dye, AlexaFluor647® (AF647). 25 kDa PEI-UCNPs achieved highest LT-estimated FRET efficiencies of ~11% in H 2 O and 16% in D 2 O, respectively. These findings highlight that polymer MW should be considered when optimising UCNP synthesis.
items.authors: Rebecca McGonigle, Christian Homann, Ciera Connelly, Marta Gajewska, Niko Hildebrandt, Robert Pal

items.title: PtSe2/Graphene Interfacial Coupling Enhances the Intrinsic Electrocatalytic Activity of PtSe2 Edge Sites
items.abstract: Platinum-based chalcogenides (PtX2) can be efficiently activated as electrocatalysts for water splitting through the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Edges in layered PtSe2 are effective in HER; however, the effect of edge interaction with conductive electrodes like graphene remains unclear. This study investigates the mechanism by which PtX2 (X = S, Se, Te) edges interact with graphene to uncover the origin of chalcogen-dependent differences in electrocatalysis through interfacial electronic coupling. Graphene flakes decorated with PtX2 nanosheets have reduced overpotential and enhanced kinetics in the HER. Interestingly, PtSe2/graphene exhibits the lowest overpotential among all samples, even though it also has the lowest electrochemically accessible surface area. First-principles calculations confirm the interfacial coupling between PtSe2 edges and graphene with pronounced charge accumulation in platinum-selenium edges. Gibbs free energy calculations show different activities for different chalcogens of PtX2/graphene, consistent with experimental results. Our findings indicate that graphene acts as an electronic regulator for PtSe2/graphene, which enhances the intrinsic catalytic activity of the platinum-selenium edge sites, making them more effective for the HER despite their lower density. This interfacial electronic coupling through conductive electrodes provides a powerful strategy for the rational design of next-generation electrocatalysts, enabling enhanced activity and selectivity in advanced electrochemical systems.
items.authors: Ilias M. Oikonomou, Axel Zuber, Apostolos Koutsioukis, Iva Plutnarová, Zdenek Sofer, Michelle P. Browne

items.title: Asymmetric Electrical Double Layer Charging in Ionomers under Pure Water
items.abstract: Electrode interfaces with ionic polymers (ionomers) create local microenvironments in membrane electrolysis and other applications, yet the formation and dynamics of electrical double layers (EDLs) at ionomer|electrode interfaces are incompletely understood. Unlike traditional aqueous electrolytes with both mobile cations and anions, ionomer interfaces couple mobile counterion motion to the slower response of tethered polymer-backbone ionic groups. Studying these solid|ionomer interfaces, with pure water feed as in many technology applications, is more difficult than with conventional electrolytes due to the lack of a liquid supporting electrolyte for simple integration of counter and reference electrodes. Here, we use a membrane-electrode-assembly-inspired architecture with a lateral ionomer strip and a salt-bridged reference electrode to independently track anodic and cathodic potentials while sweeping the voltage between the two Pt-solid|ionomer interfaces in pure water. We quantify electrode-resolved non-faradaic charging and show that fixed polymer charges and mobile counterions contribute differently to interfacial capacitance. In anion-exchange ionomers, mobile Cl- responds rapidly, whereas fixed quaternary ammonium groups relax more slowly, producing a capacitance asymmetry. This asymmetry weakens when sufficient time is allowed for relaxation and is suppressed by supporting electrolyte. When Nafion cation-exchange ionomer is used instead, the results show a reversal in the sign of the asymmetry. Supporting molecular dynamics simulations establish coupled counterion motion and tethered-charge relaxation as governing features of pure-water ionomer EDLs. The work thus provides a framework for studying and ultimately designing ionomer microenvironments for membrane electrolysis and other applications. The Bigger Picture Pure-water-fed membrane electrolyzers rely on ionomers to carry charge to catalyst surfaces. Unlike soluble liquid electrolytes, ionomers contain mobile counterions and oppositely charged groups fixed to a polymer chain. The details of how these charges form electrical double layers under positive and negative polarization are not fully understood. We developed a model cell with a solid ionomer electrolyte that senses each electrode potential separately during cell operation. The measurements show asymmetric, time-dependent charging in pure water, with mobile counterions responding more rapidly than polymer-bound charge. Added electrolytes suppress this charging-rate imbalance; reversing the ionomer charge sign also reverses the asymmetry of the charging response, and a custom-synthesized more-flexible polymer backbone reduces the rate dependence of the apparent capacitance. The work here shows how the ionomer is an active part of the electrochemical interface, in addition to an ion conductor in the bulk. The platform and fundamental principles developed here are relevant to water electrolyzers, fuel cells, and other membrane-based electrochemical devices.
items.authors: Yunseok Kang, Fabrice Roncoroni, Andrew D. Pendergast, Wenbo Zhang, Mei-Chen Kuo, Ahmet Kusoglu

items.title: Helium Compression Chamber: an ab initio molecular dynamics approach to chemical reactions under pressure
items.abstract: Understanding how pressure affects chemical reactivity requires methods capable of describing both the structural response of molecules and the thermodynamics of reactions under compression. We present the Helium Compression Chamber (HeCC), a computational approach in which molecules are compressed within an explicit helium environment and their reaction free energy profiles are determined from finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations. An on-the-fly machine-learning force field is employed to make extensive sampling feasible while retaining ab initio accuracy for the underlying potential-energy evaluations. The pressure response of four representative reactions is investigated, including bond cleavage, electrocyclization, cycloaddition, and hydrogen transfer. The calculated free-energy profiles show that compression systematically favors reactions associated with a decrease in molecular volume, while the opposite trend is observed for cyclobutene ring opening. In particular, the Diels–Alder reaction becomes barrierless at sufficiently high pressure, whereas the barriers for hexatriene cyclization and the 1,5-hydrogen shift decrease progressively with compression. The structural changes along the reaction coordinates and the pressure dependence of the corresponding activation and reaction volumes are compared with predictions from the extreme pressure-polarizable continuum model (XP-PCM) method. The comparison illustrates both the consistency and the differences between explicit-and continuum-pressure descriptions. HeCC therefore offers a route toward finite-temperature simulations of chemical reactions under pressure and provides a foundation for extending such calculations to more realistic solvation environments.
items.authors: Jorge Laranjeira, Roberto Cammi, Maximilian Amsler, Bo Chen

items.title: Novel Quinoxaline-Based Cyanocarbonimidodithioate Derivatives as Non-Hydroxamate Selective HDAC8 Inhibitors: Design, Synthesis, Biological Evaluation and Mechanistic Studies
items.abstract: Histone deacetylase 8 (HDAC8) has emerged as a promising anticancer target; however, most clinically approved hydroxamate-based HDAC inhibitors possess several limitations. A novel series of quinoxaline-based HDAC inhibitors containing a sulfur-based cyanocarbonimidodithioate non-hydroxamate zinc-binding group was designed and synthesized to overcome the selectivity and toxicity limitations of conventional hydroxamate HDAC inhibitors. A total of twenty-three quinoxaline-cyanocarbonimidodithioate derivatives (QZ 1-23) were synthesized and evaluated for HDAC8 inhibitory activity. The compounds demonstrated preferential inhibition of HDAC8 over HDAC4. Among the series, QZ-11 (IC50 = 0.3 μM) and QZ-4 (IC50 = 0.57 μM) emerged as the most promising inhibitors exhibiting favourable selectivity profiles against other tested HDAC isoforms. Both compounds demonstrated moderate to good antiproliferative activity against the IMR-32, SH-SY5Y, and FaDu cell lines. Biological studies revealed that QZ-4 and QZ-11 significantly suppressed colony formation, induced apoptosis, activated caspase-3/7, and induced G2/M phase cell-cycle arrest in IMR-32 cells, and increased acetylation of the HDAC8 substrate SMC3 without altering total SMC3 expression. Molecular docking studies suggested key interactions with HDAC8 selectivity-determining residues His142, Tyr306, and Phe152, while molecular dynamics simulations revealed stable occupancy of the catalytic pocket and persistent Zn-associated interactions throughout 100 ns trajectories. Collectively, these findings identify quinoxaline-cyanocarbonimidodithioates as a promising class of non-hydroxamate HDAC8- inhibitors and support further optimization of sulfur-based zinc-binding pharmacophores for the development of next-generation epigenetic anticancer agents.
items.authors: Kosana Sai Chaitanya, Dharani Sen, Markus Schweipert, Srinuvasu Nakka, Muzaffar-Ur-Rehman Mohammed, Katja Ohlemüller

items.title: An Algorithm for computing Three- and Four-Body Density Matrices from CASCI Wavefunction and AI-Assisted Code Optimization
items.abstract: Three- and four-body reduced density matrices in the active space are required for second-order n-electron valence perturbation theory (NEVPT2) following complete active-space configuration interaction (CASCI) calculations. We developed an algorithm to generate these computationally demanding quantities by extending the pi-CASCI program, which is based on the graphical symmetric group approach (GSGA). A manually written prototype was subsequently optimized through AI-assisted code optimization, resulting in substantially improved performance.
items.authors: Kiyoshi Tanaka, Takahiro Katagiri, Tatsuya Nakano, Yuji Mochizuki

items.title: Spatially-Resolved Viscoelastic Response with AFM-IR
items.abstract: The viscoelastic response of phase-separated polymers systems may deviate from bulk values at the nanoscale. However, current measurement techniques lack the resolution to unmask local variations. We previously demonstrated the advantages of using a focused, pulsed infrared (IR) laser to photothermally heat a sample locally during nanomechanical measurements with an atomic force microscope (AFM), with heating controlled by varying the laser repetition rate. Herein, we demonstrate this IR heating coupled with nano-Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (nDMA). First, we measured the storage and loss modulus of a homogenous copolymer at varying IR repetition rates (i.e., at varying sample temperature), demonstrating a viscoelastic modulus response that is typical near the glass transition temperature. Further, we varied the IR laser repetition rate while modulating the AFM probe between 5 Hz and 100 Hz. With time-temperature superposition, modulus master curves were constructed through the Williams-Landel-Ferry relation, and the shift factors of IR heating-coupled nDMA curves were used to estimate the relation between IR repetition rate and surface temperatures. Lastly, this technique was applied to a phase-separated polymer blend to demonstrate the utility of the technique to decouple the viscoelastic behavior of different phases by leveraging the high spatial resolution of AFM.
items.authors: Carina Yi Jing Lim, Jeffrey J. Schwartz, Bede Pittenger, Yuran Shi, Yoko Tomo, Peter De Wolf

items.title: Symmetry Numbers: A Flexible Approach for Molecules and Transition States
items.abstract: Symmetry numbers are essential corrections in thermochemistry and chemical kinetics, but their reliable assignment remains difficult in automated workflows, especially for stereochemical, fluxional, cyclic, and transition-state structures. We present a stereochemistry-aware automorphism (SAA) approach for computing symmetry numbers using the StereoMolGraph (SMG) framework. In this representation, local stereodescriptors encode rigid local geometries directly in the molecular graph, so the symmetry number is obtained as the order of the automorphism group that preserves both connectivity and encoded stereochemistry. This avoids the need for a post hoc “label stereocenter” correction and provides a direct graph-theoretical analogue of permutation-based symmetry number definitions. Model dependence is handled explicitly by choosing which molecular features are treated as fixed or fluxional, enabling consistent treatment of rigidity, free rotation, umbrella inversion, and pseudorotation assumptions. Beyond overall molecular and transition-state symmetry numbers, the same framework yields external and internal symmetry numbers for hindered-rotor treatments, including an effective external symmetry number for cases where the overall symmetry number is non-separable. Benchmark calculations reproduce the expected symmetry numbers for all supported benchmark molecules and resolve cases where existing rule-based or corrected-connectivity approaches fail, including stereochemically distinct structures with identical connectivity. The SAA approach is highly robust, making it suitable for automated thermochemical and kinetic modeling of molecules and reactions.
items.authors: Maxim Papusha, Andreas V. Copan, Brandon Rotavera, Kai Leonhard

items.title: The Critical Role of Water in Safe, Scalable Diboron-Mediated Nitro Reductions .
items.abstract: The use of diboron compounds for nitro group reduction, an essential transformation in the synthesis of a wide range of nitrogen-containing functional groups, offers an attractive alternative to traditional methods like hydrogenation and dissolving metal reduction. This method has seen limited uptake in the literature despite avoiding transition metals and specialized equipment. Using a combination of reaction calorimetry and kinetic analysis, careful selection of the reaction solvent, diboron source, and inclusion of water enabled the identification of safe and simple conditions for reduction of nitro groups. The scope of the reaction is broad under mild conditions where water plays a critical role in driving reactivity while maintaining wide safety margins.
items.authors: Yilin Cao, Matthew Joannou, Michael Mandler, Sergey Melnikov, Iulia Teleuca, Shasha Zhang

items.title: Dynamic Reactant Forcing Circumvents CO Poisoning in Catalytic CO Oxidation
items.abstract: Heterogeneous catalysts are usually optimized under static feed conditions, forcing a compromise between reactant adsorption, surface reaction, and site regeneration. For CO oxidation on Pt, this compromise is especially severe because CO binds strongly and suppresses O2 activation. Here we show that externally imposed square-wave modulation of the CO pressure can break this static limitation on Pt(111). Using synchronized infrared reflection absorption spectroscopy and mass spectrometry under constant O2 background, we directly resolve the coupled evolution of CO∗ coverage and CO2 production during each forcing cycle. CO introduction produces an initial CO2 burst followed by CO poisoning, whereas CO removal generates a second CO2 burst as vacant sites reopen O2 dissociation pathways. A Langmuir–Hinshelwood microkinetic model reproduces these transients and identifies the optimum forcing window as a balance between CO replenishment, CO desorption, and O2 activation on regenerated sites. Model-guided experimentation indicates the most favorable regimes of forcing frequency and duty cycle. At 475 K and PO2 = 5 × 10−5 mbar, the strongest tested protocol (approximately 0.3 s CO-on and 0.7 s CO-off) gives an approximately threefold larger time-averaged normalized m/z = 44 signal than continuous CO exposure at the same temperature, O2 pressure, and peak CO pressure. These results provide direct experimental evidence that reactant forcing can access productive non-steady-state surface coverages unavailable under static operation, establishing a mechanistic framework for programmable catalytic rate enhancement.
items.authors: Esteban L. Fornero, Eliseo Perez Gomez, Gengnan Li, Zubin Darbari, Cailey Bobadilla, Jerzy Sadowski

items.title: Rate-independent limits on a sulphating, self-renewing oxide catalyst: exact master-equation results with lattice kinetic Monte Carlo checks
items.abstract: Copper oxide takes up sulphur dioxide as a sorbent because sulphation converts it to inactive copper sulphate. Whether a copper oxide surface that sulphates in service and renews itself by exposing fresh copper can instead act as a catalyst for SO 2 oxidation is a question about site statistics as much as chemistry. We study it with a lattice model whose elementary rates are unknown, and we therefore restrict the main claims to statements that hold for every strictly positive assignment of rate constants. Three such results are established. First, under a dual-site mechanism in which O 2 adsorbs dissociatively onto a vacant nearest-neighbour pair and SO 2 onto a single site, an isolated patch of one or two active sites has a stationary product rate of exactly zero, and every connected patch of three or more sites has a strictly positive rate. This is proved and checked exhaustively on all 996 connected graphs of up to seven sites. Second, on a randomly deactivated lattice the share of surviving sites that can never turn over follows the closed form 𝐷 (𝑝) = (1 − 𝑝) 𝑧 + 𝑧𝑝(1 − 𝑝) 𝑡2 , which is 86.9% on a square lattice at 90% deactivation. Combined with exact stationary rates of every component shape, the classical cluster expansion gives the rate of a randomly deactivated surface without sampling. It shows that an earlier kinetic Monte Carlo run reporting a dead surface was a fluctuation in too short a window, on a surface that was never dead. Third, when sulphated sites are recovered only by discarding the oxide layer, the product obtained per copper atom consumed is exactly (𝑘 𝑑 /𝑘 𝑠 ) 𝑓 sulphate , bounded by the branching ratio between product release and sulphation. This quantity is the inverse cumulative site-loss selectivity of Foley, Johnson and Bhan, and a chemical regeneration channel is the only route past the bound. All stationary solutions use the Grassmann, Taksar and Heyman reduction, which we show is required. A least-squares solve used earlier was wrong by up to twelve orders of magnitude on small rates.
items.authors: Pragyaan Gaur

items.title: Extracting Latent Sequence-Function Information from Directed Evolution to Design Improved C-H Azidases
items.abstract: Directed evolution is a powerful approach for enzyme engineering, but conventional workflows use only a fraction of the information generated during experimental screening. Typically, only top-performing variants are sequenced and propagated, while sequence-function information from the remainder of the library is discarded. Here, we develop a data-efficient strategy to recover and leverage this latent information for enzyme design. Screened variants are grouped into activity-defined bins, pooled, and subjected to long-read sequencing, enabling efficient acquisition of sequence-function relationships while preserving relative activity information. Ordinal machine learning models trained on these binned data are then used to predict beneficial mutations. We applied this strategy to SadX, an engineered Fe(II)- and α-ketoglutarate-dependent azidase previously evolved for site-selective C-H azidation. Using only data from a previous directed evolution campaign, the models identified mutations that significantly improved catalytic performance. Experimental validation showed that several predicted single mutations enhanced azidation activity by up to 3-fold relative to the parent enzyme. These results demonstrate that substantial gains in enzyme activity can be achieved by extracting additional information from existing directed evolution datasets, providing a general strategy for converting routinely generated screening data into actionable sequence-function information for enzyme design.
items.authors: Ayantika Ghosh, Sameer D'Costa, Christian A. Gomez, Bryce Johnson, Prajwal Prabhu, Anthony Gitter

items.title: Distinguishing Pharmaceutical Salts and Cocrystals by Fluorescence Lifetime Mapping and Quantum Crystallography
items.abstract: Distinguishing between salt and cocrystal forms of a drug remains challenging in multicomponent systems with ambiguous proton transfer, particularly during bulk production in the pharmaceutical industry. Here, we address this challenge by combining fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) for rapid bulk-phase discrimination with Hirshfeld atom refinement (HAR) for single-crystal-level validation. This integrated FLIM–HAR approach was applied to 11 multicomponent solids derived from the pharmaceutical drugs niflumic acid, mefenamic acid, and sulfamethazine. Owing to its sensitivity to the local electronic environment and crystal-field effects, FLIM provided spatially resolved lifetime signatures that clearly distinguished salts from cocrystals, with salts consistently exhibiting longer fluorescence lifetimes. HAR unambiguously located the transferred protons, as evidenced by difference Fourier maps, thereby validating the salt–cocrystal assignments. Analysis of intermolecular interactions using the HAR models further revealed stronger interactions and tighter crystal packing in the salts, primarily arising from charge-assisted hydrogen bonding, consistent with the observed lifetime differences. The correlation between fluorescence lifetime and HAR-determined protonation state demonstrates that lifetime provides a sensitive probe of proton transfer in pharmaceutical solids. The integrated FLIM–HAR methodology therefore provides a rapid and reliable strategy for distinguishing pharmaceutical salts and cocrystals, with particular potential for bulk-phase characterization.
items.authors: Amit Kumar, Aditya Kumar Prajapati, Sofia Arefeen Khan, Monika Gupta, Sajesh P. Thomas

items.title: Mapping under-represented chalcone chemical space with an open-source Virtual Chalcone Library (VCL)
items.abstract: Chalcones are highly versatile privileged scaffolds, yet substantial regions of their synthetically accessible chemical space remain under-explored. Herein, we report an open-source Virtual Chalcone Library (VCL) comprising 489,475 unique structures generated from commercially available aromatic ketones and aldehydes using the freely available DataWarrior platform. Comparison of the VCL with a curated dataset of 8,886 literature chalcones revealed structural bias towards a small number of pharmacophore motifs, while highlighting under-represented regions of chemical space. Benzofuran-containing chalcones emerged as a prominent example and were selected as a case study for prospective exploration. Physicochemical filtering for favourable medicinal chemistry properties reduced this region to 1,181 candidates, from which diversity analysis identified 30 representative structures. Six novel chalcones were selected and successfully prepared, establishing two “synthetic outposts” in under-represented chemical space. A series of “deep-space” virtual chalcones (DS1-DS9) were identified with DS6 synthesised from commercially available starting materials. These syntheses provide experimental validation of the data-driven, VCL-guided workflow. The VCL is openly available as a community resource, accompanied by tutorials for its implementation and analysis in DataWarrior. This study establishes a framework for identifying, prioritising and experimentally accessing under-represented regions of chalcone chemical space.
items.authors: Alexander Ciupa

items.title: Persistent Alkyne-Bridged Bis-Trityl Diradicaloids with an Open-Shell Ground State
items.abstract: Organic singlet diradicaloids are of interest for spintronics, singlet fission, and quantum information science because of their electronic and magnetic properties. However, the synthesis of persistent diradicaloids with high diradical character remains a challenge. Herein, we report the synthesis of three novel alkyne-bridged diradicaloids based on a tetrathiaarylmethyl (trityl) radical. Electron Paramagnetic Resonance spectroscopy and magnetic susceptibility measurements were used to determine the spin-spin exchange interaction J in all three compounds, revealing narrow singlet-triplet gaps of -1 kcal/mol, -0.4 kcal/mol, and -0.05 kcal/mol for 1 •• , 2 •• , and 3 •• , respectively. DFT calculations support the singlet open-shell nature of the ground state in all three diradicaloids and yield a diradical character y 0 of 0.47, 0.53, and 0.76 for 1 •• , 2 •• , and 3 •• , respectively. Furthermore, low-energy absorption bands at 780 nm for 1 •• and 2 •• and at 500 nm for 3 •• show the transition between the open-shell ground state and a closed-shell cumulenic state. In addition, the reactivity of all three compounds towards oxygen is rationalized based on the spin-spin interaction. Lastly, since the molecules share similar geometries, J is found to be in inverse correlation to y 0 .This study thereby provides extensive insight into the structural relations between polyynic and cumulenic states, and the stability of tritylbased diradicaloids.
items.authors: Lars Westhofen, Andrea Pellegrini, Stefan Grimme, Olav Schiemann

items.title: Iterative Multimutant Design Creates a Family-Like Enzyme Ensemble
items.abstract: Natural enzyme families achieve functional breadth by diversifying a common scaffold into specialized enzymes. Engineering comparable family-like diversity for synthetic chemistry is challenging because directed evolution workflows frequently optimize one enzyme for one substrate at a time. Here we show that an iterative process of designing and screening energetically compatible multimutant variants can explore sequence space broadly and efficiently. Starting from weak azole N-methylation by human nicotinamide N-methyltransferase, screening only 1,600 clones over three rounds yielded an enzyme ensemble with broad scope. The generated catalysts carried up to 11 active-site substitutions and displayed mean initial-rate gains equivalent to approximately 11-fold per round, with overall gains exceeding 3,000-fold for individual enzyme-substrate pairs. Regioselectivity exceeded 99:1, preparative methylation afforded 87% isolated yield, and all thermally characterized variants were more thermostable than the wild type. Broad activity across diverse azoles emerged collectively from sequence-diverse specialist enzymes. Mapping all mutational routes between two high-activity variants showed that each passed through a lessactive intermediate, revealing why stepwise local optimization can miss high-performing variants. Thus, iteratively testing energetically compatible multimutant designs transformed one promiscuous enzyme into a family-like ensemble of complementary catalysts.
items.authors: Lucas Bocquin, Om Desai, Kateryna Zelenska, Matthias Garbrecht, Tom Hoenig, Alina Klein

items.title: Acyl-1,4-Dihydropyridines as Efficient Dual-Mode Photoinitiators for Radical Polymerisation under Blue and Green Light
items.abstract: Acyl-1,4-dihydropyridines are readily accessible radical precursors, but their poten al as photoini ators has remained largely unexplored.Here we show that these easily prepared compounds are dual-mode photoini ators that operate across the visible spectrum.Under blue light (405-475 nm), they act directly as Type I photoini ators: photoinduced fragmenta on releases acyl radicals that polymerise acrylate and methacrylate monomers.In trimethylolpropane triacrylate, DHP-2-NMe₂ and DHP-5-OMe show the highest Type I ac vity, with DHP-2-NMe₂ inducing gela on in only 6 s at a loading of 0.042 wt%.Under green light (525 nm), the DHPs serve as co-ini ators in photosensi sed Type II systems.With porphyrin-, BODIPY-and xanthene-based photosensi sers, rapid photopolymerisa on is observed; DHP-5-OMe is the most consistent co-ini ator, and PdOEP gives gela on mes of 2-14 s (median 3 s).Subs tuent-dependent reac vity observed in radical-trapping experiments supports a photoinduced electron-transfer pathway that, under op mised condi ons, delivers a Giese-type adduct in 92% yield under green light.Finally, combining DHP-1-H with I2BDP in a photopolymerisable glass increases the holographic diffrac on efficiency at 532 nm from 43% to 82% and the refrac ve-index modula on from 1.43 × 10⁻³ to 2.39 × 10⁻³.Single-step synthesis, strong visible-light absorp on and complete photobleaching make acyl-DHPs a prac cal pla orm for visible-light photopolymerisa on and holographic pa erning.
items.authors: Metodej Dvoracek, Pratik Avinash, Karthikeyan Manoharan, Arun Madathil, Luke Adams, Tatsiana Mikulchyk

items.title: Bulk Post-Polymerization Modification of a Single-Crystalline 2D Polymer via the Katritzky Reaction: A Modular Platform for Functional 2D Materials
items.abstract: Synthesizing two-dimensional polymers (2DPs) via single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) topochemical polymerization presents a dual challenge: preorganizing multifunctional monomers into two-dimensional crystal lattices and ensuring their polymerizable groups remain in close proximity to enable topochemical reaction in 2D. Consequently, topochemical 2DPs remain rare, and strategies for their post-polymerization modification, a standard tool in 1D polymer chemistry, are even more limited. Existing pyrylium-functionalized 2DPs suffer from severe steric hindrance caused by 2,6-di-tert-butyl substituents on pyrylium, restricting their post-synthetic Katritzky transformations solely to small nucleophiles like ammonia. To overcome this limitation, we synthesized a 2,6-di(isopropyl)styrylpyrylium triolefin monomer featuring 2,6-di-isopropyl substituents on pyrylium instead of 2,6di-tert-butyl. This subtle steric modification preserves topochemical polymerizability, while dramatically enhancing the reactivity of the resulting 2DP, enabling facile pore-wall functionalization with nucleophiles such as methylamine or ethylenediamine, to form Nmethyl- and N-(2-aminoethyl)pyridinium sites, respectively. Spectroscopic measurements show no detectable residual pyrylium in either derivative, while the ion-exchange capacity of the N-methyl derivative agrees with its theoretical capacity. These results establish solid-state pyrylium-to-pyridinium conversion as a strategy for post-polymerization modification of a topochemical 2DP precursor and represent a solid foundation for accessing a wide variety of topochemical 2DPs with engineered pore functionality.
items.authors: Valentin-Razvan Lupu, Antonia Neels, Paweł P. Ziemiański, Mirjana Dimitrievska, Vera Maria Kissling, Dorina M. Opris

items.title: LipidOracle: Ambiguity-aware lipid annotation across fragmentation methods
items.abstract: Tandem mass spectra (MS²) rarely determine a complete lipid structure, yet annotation software reports a best-scoring name and leaves users to judge whether the spectrum distinguishes it from other isomers. LipidOracle enumerates every isomer compatible with a precursor, converts the scores into probabilities with a softmax calibrated on standards, and reports the structural detail on which the credible candidates agree. An independent audit tests whether any observed fragment separates the reported structure from its closest rival. Annotation depth, from sum composition to double-bond position, is thus set by the evidence in each spectrum. The same inference handled collision-, electron- and ultraviolet photodissociation spectra, with only the fragment model exchanged. On standards, it located double bonds among thousands of candidate isomers with small credible sets, and in human plasma and mouse liver it named chains and double-bond positions only where the spectra supported them. The approach extends to any activation method whose fragments can be predicted.
items.authors: Vincen Wu, Abraham Moyal, Adriano Rutz, Nicola Zamboni

items.title: Oxidative strong metal-support interaction determines selectivity in supported Rh catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation
items.abstract: The restructuring of a catalyst’s interface with its support can be tailored via strong metal-support interactions (SMSI) in order to achieve desired product selectivity. SMSI is usually associated with reductive conditions, where a reduced oxide support covers a supported metal phase and alters catalytic activity. Here, pretreatment-dependent SMSI of rhodium nanoparticles supported on rutile titania is shown to control the selectivity profile for CO 2 hydrogenation reactions between methanation and the reverse water-gas shift reaction at 500 °C. Oxidative pretreatments at 400 °C were found to promote methanation with an initial rate of 5.1 mol/mol Rh /s for an O 2 pretreated sample and 5.8 mol/mol Rh /s for an O 2 followed by H 2 pretreated sample, whereas a H 2 pretreatment at 400 °C suppressed the methanation reaction to an initial rate of 0.25 mol/mol Rh /s. Instead of following classical methods of catalyst restructuring, such as sintering and reductive SMSI, the catalyst forms an SMSI overlayer under oxidative conditions, which restructures its active sites to selectively promote the methanation reaction. The effects of the restructuring are long-lived and dominated the catalyst selectivity even after more than 100 hours under reaction conditions. We demonstrate that this oxidative SMSI overlayer grows via a rhodium titanate intermediate and is necessary for creating active sites for methanation, shifting the catalyst’s selectivity away from the RWGS reaction. Theoretical calculations further demonstrate the thermodynamic favorability of TiO 2 overlayer growth under experimentally-relevant oxidative conditions. These results demonstrate that catalyst pretreatment conditions are a facile and effective tool for tuning the catalyst-support interface by allowing for the construction of an oxidative strong metal-support interaction that determines the product selectivity of supported rhodium catalysts.
items.authors: Jake Heinlein, Jake Erbez, Anastassiya Khan, Sabrina M. Gericke, Xiaobo Chen, Meng Li

items.title: GPCR–G protein structural endpoints carry evolutionarily localinformation about the captured G protein class
items.abstract: Structures of GPCR–G protein complexes are widely used to infer coupling selectivity, yet receptor coordinates in a mature complex may carry information associated with the transducer that was captured. This study analysed 1,360 experimental class A GPCR structures to ask how captured G protein class information is represented in receptor coordinates, how far it transfers across receptor families, and how receptor-only coordinate models relate to the experimental specimens they derive from. Across 207 receptor–transducer units from 169 receptors, receptor sequence and endpoint geometry both predicted the captured class (Gs, Gi/o or Gq/11) under receptor-grouped validation, but transfer declined with evolutionary separation: geometry outperformed sequence at 50% sequence identity (macro ROC AUC 0.731 versus 0.638), and both were near chance at 30%. Among 34 receptors resolved with more than one transducer family, held-out receptor geometry retained a small captured-class signal that sequence cannot provide. By contrast, a compact four-feature receptor geometry recovered the annotated active/inactive state almost completely (ROC AUC 0.996), including when close homologues were separated. Functional coupling annotation showed that more than half of the mapped units come from receptors supported for at least two G protein families, and a specimen-level audit showed that most receptor-only coordinate models derive from transducer-containing cryo-EM specimens. Receptor coordinates in mature class A GPCR complexes therefore carry distributed, evolutionarily local information about the captured G protein class. A captured structural class should not be read as an intrinsic or exclusive coupling preference, and receptor-only coordinate models should not be equated with experimentally partner-free receptors
items.authors: Hossein Batebi

items.title: Bio-based furan- and bifuran-containing dilinoleic dimethacrylates: synthesis, photocuring, and network properties
items.abstract: Photocurable methacrylate resins are widely used in biomedical applications, but many are derived from fossil-based monomers.To enhance their renewable content, two bio-based photocurable dilinoleic derivatives incorporating either a furan or bifuran core were synthesized and comparatively evaluated.The macromonomers were prepared via transesterification of dimethyl 2,5-furandicarboxylate or dimethyl 2,2'-bifuran 5,5'-dicarboxylate with dilinoleic diol, followed by methacrylation of the resulting hydroxyl-terminated intermediates.Successful esterification and methacrylate functionalization were confirmed by 1 H NMR and FT-IR spectroscopy, while 1 H NMR integration signals revealed methacrylation degrees of 81% and 75% for the furan-and bifuran-containing macromonomers, respectively.Rheological analysis revealed viscosities of ~8 and ~16 Pa•s for the furan-and bifuran-based macromonomers, respectively, enabling direct photocuring without reactive diluents.Photo-DSC analysis demonstrated faster photopolymerization of the furan-based macromonomer, whereas the bifuran analogue exhibited slower curing kinetics, particularly under ambient atmospheric conditions.13 C CP MAS NMR analysis of the photocured materials confirmed the formation of crosslinked polymer networks.UV curing yielded predominantly amorphous, flexible polymer networks with low glass transition temperatures (Tg) near -24 °C and high gel fractions (86 ± 1.2% and 88 ± 0.2%).Bifuran-based networks showed better mechanical properties (higher stiffness and flexibility), while both furan-and bifuran-based materials preserved favorable cell viability of 87 ± 5% and 89 ± 4%, respectively.Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of both renewable macromonomers as photocurable matrices for biomedical applications.
items.authors: Amna Sadiq, Agata Goszczyńska, Miroslawa El Fray

items.title: Probing Nanoscale Carrier Dynamics in P3HT Blended with a Non-Fullerene Acceptor: Impact of Mixing on Device-Relevant Carrier Generation
items.abstract: High-performing organic photovoltaics (OPVs) rely not only on the appropriate energetics and interfaces for separating excitons into charges, but on distinct areas of donor-rich and acceptor-rich domains to transport those charges to electrodes once separated. In this work, we study a bulk heterojunction (BHJ) of well-studied poly(3-hexylthiophene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT) and a non-fullerene acceptor with an A1-D-A2-D-A1 motif, octyl rhodanine-thiophene-benzothiadiazole-thiophene-octyl rhodanine (ORTBT). Using device characterization and time-resolved spectroscopic techniques, we show that despite promising picosecond photophysical properties P3HT:ORTBT blends do not lead to long-lived charges due to overly-imbalanced mixing between the ORTBT acceptor and P3HT donor on length scales that are either too small or too large. We compare results with a prototypical BHJ, P3HT and PC61BM fullerene to understand the photophysical differences in the exciton dissociation dynamics. The significant mixing in P3HT:ORTBT disrupts the crystalline regions of the P3HT that are necessary for effective hole transport. This work demonstrates the need to consider both the chemical and physical properties of non-fullerene acceptors to achieve an optimal balance of donor-acceptor mixing that facilitates high exciton dissociation efficiency and long-lived carrier transport pathways in the bulk.
items.authors: Bryon W. Larson, Melissa K. Gish, Unsal Koldemir, David P. Ostrowski, Kathryn A. O’Hara, Sean E. Shaheen

items.title: Majority-Rule of Enantiomeric Excess in Chiral Halide Perovskites for continuous tuning of chiroptical properties
items.abstract: Chiral halide perovskites have emerged as promising platform for spin-optoelectronic applications, yet the role of chiral precursor composition in governing their chiroptical properties remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how enantiomeric excess (ee) controls the chiroptical response of the prototypical two-dimensional (2D) chiral halide perovskite (R/S-MBA)2PbI4 (MBA = methylbenzylammonium) across a compositional series spanning ee = -100% to +100% corresponding to R-MBA mole fractions ranging from 0% to 100%. By combining experimental spectroscopy with first-principles simulations, an approach we demonstrate to be transferable to tin-based analogues as well, we establish a quantitative structure-chiroptical property relationship across the full ee range. Circular dichroism (CD) spectra and absorption dissymmetry factors (gabs) exhibit a progressive, nonlinear evolution with increasing ee, consistent with cooperative majority-rule behavior governing chirality transfer from the organic cation to the inorganic framework. This effect is most pronounced in the 400-450 nm spectral region, where the CD signal tracks enantiomeric composition with high fidelity. Ab initio molecular dynamics coupled with time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) quantitatively reproduces both the experimental CD spectra and gabs values across the entire compositional series, revealing that the macroscopic chiroptical response originates from the collective arrangement of chiral ligands, acting as a continuous dial for simultaneously modulating optical activity. This positions the ee as a general, accessible design parameter for chiroptical engineering across the family of halide perovskites.
items.authors: Mariagrazia Fortino, Hongki Kim, Amina Alehyane, Florent Barbault, Antonio Monari, Sascha Feldmann

items.title: Asymmetric selectivity at the glycoprotein hormone receptor allosteric site
items.abstract: Position 7.42 of the glycoprotein hormone receptors has been proposed as the determinant of mutual selectivity between LHCGR and FSHR, but has not been tested reciprocally. We compared the allosteric pockets of LHCGR with Org 43553 (PDB 7FIH) and FSHR with Cpd-21f (PDB 8I2G), and mapped each ligand into the other receptor by transmembrane superposition. Seven of 27 aligned contact positions diverge, a rate not distinguishable from the transmembrane background, and the mapping is markedly asymmetric. Cpd-21f placed in LHCGR makes a 2.31 Å contact with Tyr612, against 3.69 Å for the native His615 contact, and this is the single worst contact in the molecule. Org 43553 placed in FSHR meets no comparable barrier: 21 of 23 native contacts are preserved, burial increases, and the only sequence-driven loss is a hydroxyl-to-methyl van der Waals contact. Position 7.42 therefore excludes FSHR-selective ligands from LHCGR but does not explain why Org 43553 is weaker at FSHR. We further show that the morpholine tail of Org 43553 is buried rather than solvent-exposed and contacts only residues shared between the two receptors, accounting for published structure–activity data in which extensive variation of that tail failed to shift the LH:FSH ratio. A survey of ten orthologs identifies Phe515, the closest divergent contact and the only contact-shell position where LHCGR differs from a residue both paralogs share, as primate-specific; every non-primate examined, including all standard preclinical species, carries the paralog leucine. Finally, this pocket defeats several widely used scoring functions, which rank a reciprocal head-to-tail decoy above the crystallographic pose.
items.authors: Patrick Nasser

items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Nickel-Plated Steel Wool and Nickel Strip Electrodes for Hydrogen Production from Non-Potable Water Sources
items.abstract: Traditional water electrolysis imposes a significant freshwater demand. This study evaluates alternative non-potable feedstocks to reduce this dependency. We present a comparative performance analysis of user-fabricated, three-dimensional (3D) porous nickel-plated steel wool scaffolds versus conventional flat nickel control strips. Testing was conducted across tap water, rainwater, and greywater utilizing a near-neutral sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) electrolyte. Operational performance was quantified via volumetric hydrogen (H2) yield, Faradaic efficiency, and cost-normalized output (mL/$). The porous electrode significantly outperformed the flat strip, increasing Faradaic efficiency by 7% in tap water and 5% in rainwater. Furthermore, the 3D scaffold achieved up to an 8.7× greater hydrogen yield per dollar. These results demonstrate the bench-scale feasibility of low-cost, structured electrodes for reducing freshwater dependence in water electrolysis.
items.authors: Kyle Liou

items.title: Piezoelectricity-Induced Mechanical Bond Formation in Solid-state Using Mechanochemistry
items.abstract: Mechanochemistry, long promoted as a sustainable route to chemical synthesis, remains difficult to apply predictably to complex reactions due to a limited atomic-level understanding of how mechanical energy drives reactivity. Here, we demonstrated how piezoelectric polarization in tetragonal BaTiO3 directs solid-state mechanoredox chemistry, enabling electrode-free, reductant-free and solvent-free synthesis, for forming complex mechanically interlocked molecules for the first time. During ball milling, mechanically activated tetragonal BaTiO3 nanoparticles generate spatially separated redox sites that reduce viologen building blocks, promoting radical-pairing-driven pseudorotaxane formation and subsequent formation of stable [2] rotaxanes. First-principles calculations on BaTiO3 identify shear deformation as the dominant mechanical stimulus, where strain-induced polarization field produces an energetically favorable surface potential for the coupled redox reactions. These findings for the first time establish a direct mechanistic link between mechanical deformation, piezoelectric polarization, and mechanical bond formation, providing a predictive framework for sustainably constructing complex mechanically interlocked molecular architectures through piezoelectricity-mediated mechanochemistry.
items.authors: Surojit Bhunia, Pramita Kundu, Long Zhang, Sudipto Sinha, Partha J Das, Guangcheng Wu

items.title: Ultramild conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline mediated by metal organic alloy NiGraf in green solvent
items.abstract: The conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline can be carried out under ultramild conditions (35 °C under N2 at ambient pressure) with a 40% molar excess of hydrazine as reducing agent mediated by metal-organic alloy NiGraf in aqueous tetrahydrofuran, a green solvent. Conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline will optimally employ the stable and recyclable form of the NiGraf, consisting of reduced graphene oxide entrapped in jamborite nanoparticles, in renewable solvent system H2O/THF.
items.authors: Mario Orgnoni, Rosaria Ciriminna, Enrique Rodríguez-Castellón, Giuseppina Cerrato, Mario Pagliaro, Cristina Della Pina

items.title: Donor–Acceptor Integration Modulates Reverse Intersystem Crossing in Multi-Resonant TADF Emitters
items.abstract: Multi-resonant thermally activated delayed fluorescent (MR-TADF) compounds are attractive as emitters in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) owing to their high photoluminescence quantum yields and narrowband emission. However, these emitters generally have moderate reverse intersystem crossing rate constants (kRISC), which causes triplet exciton accumulation and leads to, amongst other excitonic processes, triplet-triplet annihilation. This process results in significant efficiency roll-off in OLEDs at high luminance. Here, we report the photophysical properties of a 2 boron–nitrogen doped MR-TADF emitter, tCzBN, and two of its derivatives, SpAc-tCzBN and TRZ-SpAc-DBN, using time-resolved absorption and emission spectroscopy. Kinetic modelling of their photophysical behavior reveals that combining a donor–acceptor core with the MR-TADF moiety in TRZ-SpAc-DBN results in a higher kRISC than tCzBN and its donor-appended analog, SpAc-tCzBN, while preserving the narrowband emission of the MR-TADF unit. We attribute this enhancement to the lower effective adiabatic singlet–triplet energy gap (∆EST) and stronger spinorbit coupling in this molecular design.
items.authors: Pratiksha Dad, Kittimeth Thammanatpong, Mahni Fatahi, Peter M W Gill, Eli Zysman-Colman, Girish Lakhwani

items.title: Parameter Recovery and Noise Sensitivity of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Michaelis–Menten Kinetics: A Benchmark Against Classical Nonlinear Least Squares
items.abstract: This study evaluates a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for estimating Michaelis–Menten kinetic parameters from sparse and noisy concentration–time observations. The investigated system follows the ordinary differential equation , with a true maximum reaction rate of , Michaelis constant , initial substrate concentration , and a simulation duration of 10 time units. Synthetic observations were generated using numerical integration and additive Gaussian noise at 1% and 5% levels. The PINN consisted of a fully connected neural network with three hidden layers, 32 hidden units, and hyperbolic tangent activation functions. Its trainable kinetic parameters were constrained to positive values using the softplus transformation. Training minimized a weighted combination of data error, initial-condition error, and differential-equation residual error. To address optimization instability, the study used an increased training budget of up to 8000 epochs, early stopping, multiple initialization seeds, and cross-validation for selecting the physics-loss weight. A classical nonlinear least-squares estimator was used as a comparison method. In a diagnostic example, the corrected PINN produced errors of 1.04% for and 5.10% for , compared with 2.99% and 19.32% for the classical method. However, across the small benchmark of 18 replicates, the classical method generally achieved lower median errors and lower prediction RMSE, especially under 5% noise. The results show that the PINN can recover kinetic parameters accurately in favorable conditions, but its performance remains sensitive to data quantity, noise, optimization, and experimental design.
items.authors: Mateen Ur Rehman

items.title: Analysis of fine-tuned foundation interatomic potentials and their knowledge distillation into a cluster expansion for Ni–Pt ordering thermodynamics
items.abstract: Predicting alloy ordering thermodynamics requires the energies of thousands of atomic arrangements at fixed composition, far more than density functional theory (DFT) can routinely provide. Fine-tuned foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are a promising alternative, but whether they resolve the small energy differences between arrangements has not been established. Here, we examine this for fcc Ni–Pt in three steps. First, six foundation MLIPs fine-tuned on the same DFT data are evaluated on a 64-structure DFT benchmark. All six reach low global errors (2-20 meV/atom), but these errors are dominated by a composition-dependent offset that cancels between arrangements of one composition. We therefore evaluate the configurational energy Econf, the energy of a structure relative to the other structures of the same composition. After relaxation only four models reproduce DFT Econf (R2conf = 0.93-0.94), whereas fine-tuned eqV2 and CHGNet do not (0.48 and 0.37). Second, we locate the source of this failure. Linear probes on the frozen embeddings of all six models recover EconfDFT (R2 = 0.87 to 0.98), showing that the learned representations are intact. The accuracy is lost during relaxation: through the cell response of eqV2 and through inaccurate forces near the energy minimum in CHGNet. Third, we use the most accurate model, fine-tuned eqV3, as a teacher for knowledge distillation into a cluster expansion. Trained on 6,434 MLIP energies instead of 64 DFT energies, the distilled cluster expansion reduces the held-out DFT error from 4.43 to 2.79 meV/atom and reproduces the DFT-based transition temperatures within 167 K, comparable to the 120 K statistical uncertainty of the DFT-trained expansion itself. These results establish when fine-tuned foundation MLIPs can be trusted for alloy ordering and provide a route for transferring their accuracy to thermodynamic simulations.
items.authors: Jungjae Hwang, Jaejun Lee, Channyung Lee, Elif Ertekin, Kyoungmin Min

items.title: An Algorithm for computing Three- and Four-Body Density Matrices from CASCI Wavefunction and AI-Assisted Code Optimization
items.abstract: Three- and four-body reduced density matrices in the active space are required for second-order n-electron valence perturbation theory (NEVPT2) following complete active-space configuration interaction (CASCI) calculations. We developed an algorithm to generate these computationally demanding quantities by extending the pi-CASCI program, which is based on the graphical symmetric group approach (GSGA). A manually written prototype was subsequently optimized through AI-assisted code optimization, resulting in substantially improved performance.
items.authors: Kiyoshi Tanaka, Takahiro Katagiri, Tatsuya Nakano, Yuji Mochizuki

items.title: Where the vibronic coupling lies: promoting-mode frequencies and second-order rate theory for reverse intersystem crossing in multiresonance TADF emitters
items.abstract: Rate models for reverse intersystem crossing in multiresonance delayed-fluorescence emitters usually place the vibrational spectrum on one promoting mode near 75 meV and treat the triplet–triplet vibronic coupling at second order. Neither approximation has been tested at scale. This work computes nonadiabatic couplings and signed spin–orbit vectors (PBE0/def2-SVP, Tamm–Dancoff) for all 121 emitters of the Hagai et al. compilation, and full vibrational spectra for 17 of them. The coupling-weighted promoting quantum has a median of 173 meV, in the aromatic ring-stretch region, with about 25 modes carrying 90% of the squared coupling. Collapsing the spectrum onto a 75 meV oscillator inflates the coupling by a factor of 1.5, and second-order theory then fails: over 120 emitters its rate departs from exact diagonalisation of the vibronic problem by a median of 0.49 orders of magnitude and lies further from experiment. At the computed 173 meV the median departure is 0.10 orders, although 21 emitters still differ by more than an order. On a multimode model that preserves the residual coupling matrix it falls to 0.02 orders for the 17 emitters with spectra, against 0.61 and 0.23 orders for the single-mode model on the same molecules. Both multimode treatments overestimate the measured rate for 15 of the 17 emitters, by a median of 1.2 orders, so the remaining error lies in inputs they share. For these emitters the breakdown of second-order theory comes from the single-mode reduction; the near-resonant regime remains to be tested with full spectra.
items.authors: Ramarao Tata

items.title: ProtMutMap: Predicting Protein Binding Free Energy Changes Using Multiple-Mutation Networks
items.abstract: Predicting changes in binding free energy ΔΔ G caused by multiple mutations at protein−protein interfaces requires accounting for nonadditive interactions between mutations, which an additive approximation based on single mutations cannot capture, and for the dependence on the computational pathway in stepwise approaches that introduce mutations sequentially. Here, we propose ProtMutMap, a method that integrates information from multiple pathways in a network whose nodes represent target variants and variants containing subsets of their mutations, and whose edges represent free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations for residue substitutions. ProtMutMap simultaneously estimates the binding ΔΔ G of each variant from all edge values using Huber loss. We compared ProtMutMap with the additive approximation and the stepwise method at 30 evaluation points, including intermediate variants, using a multiple-mutation dataset comprising 7 protein complex systems derived from SKEMPI2. ProtMutMap achieved a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 1.13 kcal/mol, lower than that of either comparison method. ProtMutMap also yielded lower prediction errors than Rosetta flex ddG. These comparisons with experimental values demonstrate that integrating multiple pathways through variants containing subsets of the target mutations improves binding ΔΔ G predictions for protein variants with multiple mutations.
items.authors: Kairi Furui, Masahito Ohue

items.title: Localized Sequential Backflow Ansatz for Scalable Neural Quantum States
items.abstract: Neural Quantum State Architectures have been shown to have high accuracy on a variety of molecular and lattice systems, often outperforming traditional methods. This work replaces the all-to-all paradigm of current neural quantum states with a localized recurrent sequential backflow mechanism. Results have empirically exhibited approximately quadratic wall-clock scaling over the system sizes tested, namely the hydrogen chain with atom with length of H 10 to H 400 , suggesting a viable path towards a scalable Neural Quantum State.
items.authors: Dylan Liu-Walter

items.title: Less is more in mixture modeling: every molecular vector is a map, yet the mixture is the territory
items.abstract: Predicting mixture properties is a key challenge across domains, yet current deep-learning designs approach it blindly: they largely reuse the single-molecule recipe, compressing each molecule into a vector and predicting the mixture’s property from these vectors. We find that mixtures, as components multiply, depend increasingly on precise topological information. We therefore advocate a new design: model the mixture directly as a unified atomic system with complete and precise molecular topology. A simple instantiation of this design reaches or approaches the best published baselines across diverse domains, and indicates that the failures of existing vector-based models on some tasks stem from the same thing: every molecular vector is a map, yet the mixture is the territory.
items.authors: Xiao Yang, Guanghao Song, Zihan Xu, Yanan Yang, Baojiang He, Lingbo Ji

items.title: Biomimetic remodelling of lipid membranes using DNA nanostructures
items.abstract: The remodelling of biological membranes underpins a diverse range of sophisticated cellular processes, from cell crawling to mitosis to pathogen infection cycles. A refined understanding of the biophysical principles governing lipid bilayer remodelling is necessary to engineer ever-more advanced behaviours in microrobots, like synthetic cells, with disruptive applications in both fundamental biology and advanced biotechnology. Owing to its ability to afford control over structural and functional properties at the nano-scale, DNA nanotechnology has emerged as a prime toolkit to engineer, program, and host biomimetic responses within lipid bilayer membranes. This Perspective review surveys advances on biomimetic membrane remodelling pathways coordinated by DNA nanostructures. I discuss strategies to prescribe the interactions of DNA nanostructures with lipid bilayers, and summarise progress to drive membrane remodelling events including lateral patterning, out-of-plane restructuring, fusion, and scission. Finally, I discuss current challenges alongside the yet untapped potential of nucleic acid nanostructures in membrane bioengineering to coordinate sophisticated behaviours in synthetic cells.
items.authors: Roger Rubio Sánchez

items.title: IRexp: A database of experimental infrared band lists from open literature
items.abstract: IRexp is a collection of experimental infrared band lists (cm⁻¹ peak positions) mined from open chemistry literature, with author-reported ¹H/¹³C NMR strings and resolved structures where available. The research corpus holds 121,233 records from the PMC Open Access Subset and the Chemotion repository, including 57,646 structure-linked entries and 39,118 IR + ¹H + ¹³C + structure quadruples. The public dataset of record contains 88,519 CC-BY/CC0 records released under CC-BY-4.0, with ShareAlike and non-commercial records distributed separately under their source licences. Every record carries a source identifier and a per-record licence stamp. Technical validation covers automated transcription, recall-proxy, and consistency audits. IRexp targets multimodal training, retrieval, and structure-elucidation tools that need structured, attributable experimental peak lists.
items.authors: Ilkham Yabbarov, Rudra Sondhi, Rodrigo A. Vargas-Hernández

items.title: Hyperfine dynamics as an internal control of reactive-oxygen-species output in a triplet-born flavin–superoxide radical pair
items.abstract: When reduced flavin is activated by molecular oxygen it forms a spin-correlated radical pair—a flavin semiquinone and superoxide (O₂•⁻)—born in the triplet manifold, because ground-state O₂ is a triplet. Its singlet/triplet recombination gates the branching of reactive oxygen species, and the pair is realised in the electron-transfer flavoprotein, whose output is field-dependent. Radical-pair theory almost always treats the hyperfine tensor as fixed and the field as the variable. We invert that: with the field held fixed, what upper bound does a time-dependent active-site hyperfine coupling place on the singlet yield? We pose a coefficient inverse problem with the principal-axis components Aₖ,ₐ(t) as the control and solve it for the genuine triplet-born flavin pair (two ¹⁴N at I = 1, three protons; dimension 288) at a 200 ns lifetime. A time-dependent coupling raises the yield to ΦS = 0.290 at 50 µT, against 0.241 for the best constant coupling in the same admissible set (1.20×) and 0.203 for the molecule’s own couplings (1.43×); the reduced models give larger gains, so they overestimate the effect. The optimum places 76% of its modulation in the first 0.5 µs and is smooth and numerically near-singular, unlike the bang–bang optimum of the external-field problem. These are coherent yields obtained over a control set far larger than conformational motion can access—an upper bound on an upper bound—with spin relaxation, the dipolar coupling and the superoxide g-anisotropy left unmodelled. The falsifiable quantity is the dynamic-over-static gain, not the absolute yield.
items.authors: Pablo R. Castello, Pablo Jiménez, Carlos F. Martino

items.title: Redox-Paired Activation of Sulfur Hexafluoride Enables Nucleophilic C(sp3)–F Bond Formation
items.abstract: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is a potent greenhouse gas whose direct use as a fluorine source in organic synthesis remains underdeveloped. Here, we disclose complementary photoredox and electrochemical strategies for nucleophilic fluorinations with SF6, merging oxidative formation of carbocation intermediated from alkoxamines, carboxylic acids, or thiols with SF6 reduction, the latter providing fluoride for C(sp3)–F bond formation. The photochemical protocol efficiently converts electronrich substrates and tolerates a broad range of functional groups, whereas paired electrolysis extends the reaction to electronically deactivated substrates. Together, the two methods enable fluorination of diverse benzylic and aliphatic substrates, including late-stage fluorination of structurally complex derivatives of pharmaceuticals, natural products, and agrochemicals.
items.authors: Aniruddha Biswas, Demetra Zambardino, Tanja Gulder

items.title: CuBr-Catalyzed Enantioselective Synthesis of Decahydroquinoxaline-Based Bis(propargylamines): Application to the Synthesis of an Axially Chiral Allene
items.abstract: A CuBr-catalyzed one-pot protocol provides access to decahydroquinoxaline-based bis(propargylamines) from readily available terminal alkynes, aromatic aldehydes, and a C2symmetric chiral diamine. The three-component coupling proceeds at 120 °C within 12 h, affording the products in 58–93% yields with diastereomeric ratios of up to 99:1. The synthetic utility of the protocol is illustrated by the ZnI2-mediated conversion of a representative bis(propargylamine) (7a) into the corresponding axially chiral allene (8a) with 90% ee. This approach enables the stereoselective construction of bis(propargylamines) and demonstrates their application as precursors to axially chiral allenes.
items.authors: Laxman Alakonda, Mariappan Periasamy

items.title: Insights into Electrolyte Effects on Interfacial Kinetics and Transport in Porous Redox Flow Battery Electrodes: A Multiparadigm Modelling Study
items.abstract: Redox flow batteries (RFBs) have emerged as promising candidates for large-scale energy storage owing to their decoupled energy and power densities. Electrolyte formulation plays a key role in determining the electrochemical performance of RFBs, influencing interfacial kinetics and transport within porous electrodes. Herein, we develop a multiscale modelling framework to investigate the coupled effects of the electrolyte concentration (Methyl Viologen (MV) and NaCl) and the fibrous 3D microstructure on the porous transport and electrochemical kinetics in organic RFBs using a kinetic Monte Carlo model. We link this interfacial kinetics to the advection-diffusion transport in stochastically generated carbon felt electrode microstructures through Lattice Boltzmann Method simulations via an interpolation-based coupling. We use two performance descriptors, the fibre-averaged rate of potential loss and convective area fraction, to quantify the kinetics and transport effects, along with their interplay. While increasing MV concentration enhances the interfacial kinetics, it limits the transport within the electrode microstructure. The interfacial kinetics shows to be nontrivially governed by the supporting electrolyte. A surface area-permeability trade-off appears across microstructures with different electrolyte concentrations. This multiparadigm modelling workflow provides mechanistic insights between porous transport and interfacial electrochemical kinetics, enabling the coupled optimization of microstructures and electrolytes in RFBs.
items.authors: Avaneesh Balasubramanian, Francisco Fernandez, Alejandro A. Franco

items.title: Multigram Copper-Catalyzed Azidodeboronation of Alkenyl Boronates
items.abstract: A multigram synthetic approach to alkenyl azides based on copper-catalyzed azidodeboronation of alkenyl pinacol boronates was described.
